clinicalPearls: AGRN encodes agrin, a large proteoglycan released by the motor nerve terminal that binds LRP4 and activates MuSK to initiate postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor clustering.
Biallelic AGRN variants cause a synaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome that also disrupts maintenance of the endplate architecture and nerve-terminal integrity.
Presentation ranges from early-onset weakness to a distinctive later-onset, distal and lower-limb predominant weakness with prominent muscle atrophy that can mimic a distal myopathy or neuropathy.
Ptosis and mild ophthalmoparesis may occur, but bulbar and respiratory involvement is often less prominent than in some other subtypes.
Electrophysiology shows a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation and increased jitter, reflecting impaired transmission at structurally abnormal endplates.
Anticholinesterase medication is frequently ineffective or poorly tolerated; sympathomimetic agents such as ephedrine or salbutamol are more commonly beneficial.
Because weakness can be distal and slowly progressive with wasting, the diagnosis is easily mistaken for a hereditary neuropathy or distal myopathy without electrodiagnostic and genetic clues.
reference.pathophysiology: Agrin-related congenital myasthenic syndrome results from biallelic pathogenic variants in AGRN, which encodes agrin, a heparan-sulphate proteoglycan secreted by the motor nerve terminal into the synaptic basal lamina. Neural agrin is the master initiator of postsynaptic differentiation: it binds LRP4 in the muscle membrane, and the agrin-LRP4 complex activates MuSK, which through DOK7 and rapsyn drives dense clustering of acetylcholine receptors opposite the nerve terminal and organises the postsynaptic apparatus. Pathogenic AGRN variants impair either the receptor-clustering activity of agrin or its role in maintaining the mature neuromuscular junction, leading to disorganised, fragmented endplates, altered nerve-terminal architecture with partial denervation, and reduced acetylcholine receptor aggregation. The resulting fall in endplate potential amplitude reduces the safety margin of transmission, producing fatigable and, in many patients, distal-predominant weakness with muscle atrophy that reflects the trophic and structural consequences of chronic junctional disruption. As the defect concerns endplate formation and upkeep rather than acetylcholine hydrolysis, therapies that enhance transmission and endplate stability are favoured over anticholinesterases.
additionalDifferentials: Other postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndromes involving the same pathway, namely LRP4, MuSK and DOK7 subtypes
Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) given the distal weakness and wasting
Distal myopathies and other inherited muscle disorders
Spinal muscular atrophy and other anterior horn cell diseases
additionalInvestigations: Repetitive nerve stimulation showing a decremental response
Single-fibre electromyography demonstrating increased jitter and blocking
AGRN sequencing within a congenital myasthenic syndrome gene panel with biallelic variant confirmation
Nerve conduction studies to help distinguish the disorder from a hereditary neuropathy
Acetylcholine receptor and MuSK antibody testing to exclude autoimmune disease
Muscle imaging or biopsy where a distal myopathy is being considered
redFlags: Emerging respiratory or bulbar weakness in a previously stable patient
Rapid progression of distal weakness and wasting suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis
Deterioration after a trial of anticholinesterase medication
Recurrent falls or loss of ambulation indicating significant functional decline
reference.prognosis: The course is often slowly progressive, and while some patients maintain useful mobility with sympathomimetic therapy, others develop increasing distal weakness and atrophy over time. Respiratory involvement, when present, warrants monitoring and may influence long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the distal, atrophic phenotype as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease or a distal myopathy and missing the treatable neuromuscular junction disorder.
Relying on anticholinesterases, which are commonly ineffective or poorly tolerated in this subtype.
Assuming all congenital myasthenic syndromes present neonatally and dismissing a later-onset agrin phenotype.
Overlooking subtle decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation when the clinical picture suggests a neuropathy.
